description: Source, reservoir and cap rocks, trap structures and the environmental issues around extraction.
content_html:
How Oil and Gas Form

Petroleum (oil) and natural gas originate from the remains of marine microorganisms — mainly phytoplankton and zooplankton — that accumulated in fine-grained sediments on the sea floor over millions of years. Buried under thick piles of sediment, this organic material is subjected to increasing heat and pressure in a process called maturation. At roughly 60–120°C (the “oil window”), long-chain organic molecules crack into shorter-chain hydrocarbons: oil. At temperatures above about 150°C, lighter natural gas is produced. The rock in which the organic material matures is called the source rock.

The Three Rock Types of an Oilfield

Once generated, oil and gas migrate upward through the subsurface (being less dense than water) until they are either trapped or reach the surface and are lost. A commercial deposit requires three rock types to be present together:

The reservoir rock is where the oil or gas is stored. It must be both porous (to hold the hydrocarbons in pore spaces) and permeable (to allow the fluids to flow when drilled). Sandstones and limestones with good interconnected porosity are the most common reservoir rocks. The Brent Group sandstones of the North Sea and the Jurassic limestones of the Middle East are classic examples.

The cap rock (or seal) is a tight, impermeable rock that prevents the hydrocarbons from escaping upward. Evaporites (halite, anhydrite), unfractured shale, and mudstone are effective cap rocks. Without a cap rock, any oil that migrates into the reservoir will continue upward and be lost.

Key Fact

A commercial oilfield requires: a source rock (organic-rich, fine-grained — generates the oil); a reservoir rock (porous and permeable — stores and yields the oil); and a cap rock (impermeable — prevents upward escape). All three must be in the right spatial arrangement.

Trap Structures

A trap is any geometry that causes oil and gas to pool rather than escape. The main trap types are:

Anticline traps form where rocks have been folded into an arch (anticline). Oil and gas migrate into the crest of the fold, where they are sealed by cap rock draped over the top. The anticline is the most commonly illustrated trap in geology exams. Cross-sections in your textbook will show the dome-shaped geometry, with oil sitting above water in the reservoir rock and gas above oil at the crest.

Fault traps form where a fault brings an impermeable rock (e.g. shale) against a porous reservoir rock, sealing the migration pathway. The juxtaposition must seal tightly enough to prevent leakage. Unconformity traps occur where an impermeable layer was deposited across an eroded, tilted sequence, sealing the truncated ends of reservoir rock layers beneath. Salt dome traps form where a buoyant dome of halite (rock salt) pierces upward through overlying sediments, doming and faulting reservoir rocks around its flanks and creating a structural closure above and beside the dome.

Examiner reports repeatedly flag this confusion. Porosity is the total pore space in a rock — how much empty space it contains as a proportion of its volume. Permeability is the ability of fluids to flow through those pores — controlled by whether pores are connected to each other. A rock can be highly porous but impermeable: pumice has many pores but they are not well-connected, so fluids flow through it poorly. Conversely, a rock with moderate porosity but well-connected pores (like a well-sorted sandstone) can be highly permeable. Both properties are essential for a good reservoir rock — and permeability alone is what matters for a cap rock (it must have very low permeability to act as a seal).

Extraction Methods and Fracking

Conventional oil and gas extraction involves drilling into the reservoir rock through the cap rock; pressure in the reservoir pushes hydrocarbons up the well. As pressure declines, pumps or water injection maintain flow. Offshore extraction uses platforms drilled into the sea bed — the North Sea has over 180 oil and gas fields operated from fixed and floating platforms.

Hydraulic fracturing (fracking) is a technique used to extract oil and gas trapped in the pores of tight (very low permeability) source rocks such as shale, which are too impermeable for conventional production. High-pressure fluid is pumped into the well, fracturing the shale and propping the fractures open with sand or ceramic beads, allowing hydrocarbons to flow. Fracking has transformed oil and gas production in the United States but is controversial in the UK and elsewhere due to environmental concerns including induced seismicity, groundwater contamination risks, and methane leakage.

Key Fact

An anticline trap works because oil and gas migrate upward into the arched crest of a fold. The cap rock, draped over the crest, prevents further upward migration — trapping the hydrocarbons in the porous reservoir rock beneath. This is the most commonly examined trap type.

Onshore extraction disturbs habitats, requires access roads and pipelines, and risks blowouts and spills if well integrity fails. Offshore extraction risks catastrophic spills: the 2010 Deepwater Horizon blowout in the Gulf of Mexico released approximately 4.9 million barrels of oil, causing severe ecological damage to marine and coastal ecosystems. Gas flaring (burning off excess gas at the wellhead) releases CO₂ and black carbon. Subsidence above depleted fields can affect surface infrastructure. Fracking specifically raises concerns about water use (millions of litres per frack), disposal of contaminated fracking fluid, and small induced earthquakes caused by fluid injection affecting nearby faults. In the UK, induced seismicity was the primary reason for the moratorium on fracking operations.
exam_tip_html: Do not apply oil-trap terminology to aquifer questions. A ‘reservoir rock’ in the oil context is porous and permeable and stores hydrocarbons; a similar rock storing water is simply called a permeable aquifer — do not call it a reservoir rock in the water context, as examiners penalise cross-contamination of these terms. When asked to describe a trap, always name the trap type (anticline, fault, unconformity, salt dome), describe the geometry, and explain why oil cannot escape upward from that geometry.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Oil and gas form from marine organic material matured by heat and pressure in source rocks; they migrate upward until trapped in porous, permeable reservoir rocks beneath an impermeable cap rock.
  • The main trap types are anticlines, fault traps, unconformity traps and salt domes; each creates a different geometry that prevents upward migration of hydrocarbons.
  • Porosity (pore space) and permeability (connected flow) are distinct properties; both must be high in reservoir rocks, while cap rocks must have very low permeability to function as a seal.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the role of a cap rock in an oilfield?
A) It is the porous and permeable rock where oil is stored
B) It is the organic-rich rock where oil is generated under heat and pressure
C) It is the impermeable rock that prevents oil and gas from migrating further upward
D) It is the rock through which oil flows from the source to the trap
practice_questions.marks: C) It is the impermeable rock that prevents oil and gas from migrating further upward [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the process by which buried organic material is transformed into oil and gas.
Describe the difference between porosity and permeability in a reservoir rock.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark each for:
- Porosity is the proportion of a rock's volume made up of pore spaces (gaps between grains), expressed as a percentage. (1)
- Permeability is the ability of fluids to flow through the rock, controlled by whether the pore spaces are connected to each other. (1)

practice_questions.text: A seismic survey reveals an anticline with a crest at 2,400 m depth and the anticline limbs dipping at 15° away from the crest on each side. The oil–water contact is identified at 2,580 m depth. Calculate the maximum possible oil column thickness in metres.
practice_questions.marks:
Oil column thickness = depth of oil–water contact − depth of crest = 2,580 − 2,400 = 180 m
[2 marks: 1 for correct method, 1 for correct answer with units]

practice_questions.text: Explain how an anticline trap forms and why it can hold oil and gas in the reservoir rock.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
- Tectonic compression causes sedimentary layers to fold upward into an arch shape called an anticline. (1)
- Oil and gas, being less dense than groundwater, migrate upward through the permeable reservoir rock until they reach the crest of the arch. (1)
- An impermeable cap rock draped over the crest of the anticline prevents the hydrocarbons from escaping further upward, trapping them in the reservoir rock beneath. (1)

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the environmental impacts of extracting oil and gas from offshore fields compared with onshore fracking operations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced comparison of both extraction methods with specific impacts identified and explained; considers both local and global environmental scales; reaches a justified conclusion about relative severity.
Secure: At least two developed contrasts between offshore and onshore impacts; conclusion present.
Developing: Describes impacts of one method more fully than the other; limited comparison.
Emerging: Brief mention of one or two impacts without comparison or conclusion.

Offshore impacts:
- Catastrophic blowout risk (e.g. Deepwater Horizon 2010: ~4.9 million barrels spilled, devastating marine ecosystems).
- Routine impacts include noise pollution affecting marine mammals, disturbance of sea-bed habitats by drilling, and pipeline leaks.
- Gas flaring at wellheads releases CO₂ and black carbon, contributing to climate change.
- Subsidence above depleted offshore fields can damage sea-bed infrastructure.

Onshore fracking impacts:
- Very high water use (millions of litres per operation) stresses local freshwater supplies.
- Risk of groundwater contamination if well casing fails and fracking fluid migrates into aquifers.
- Induced seismicity from high-pressure fluid injection affecting nearby faults (key factor in UK moratorium).
- Methane leakage from poorly sealed wells contributes to greenhouse gas emissions.
- Surface habitat disturbance from well pads, roads and pipelines.

Conclusion: Both methods carry significant risks, but the nature differs: offshore blowouts risk large, acute marine disasters while fracking risks slower, localised contamination plus seismicity. Neither is risk-free; the balance of concern depends on local geology, regulatory standards, and the scale of operations. [6 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: What property must a reservoir rock have to allow oil to flow out when drilled?
Which type of trap forms where a dome of buoyant salt has pierced upward through overlying sediments?
The _____ is the organic-rich, fine-grained rock in which oil and gas are generated by maturation of buried organic material.
In hydraulic fracturing (fracking), high-pressure fluid is pumped into tight shale to create _____ through which oil or gas can flow.
Match each oilfield rock type to its key property:
right: Organic-rich and fine-grained — generates hydrocarbons under heat
Porous and permeable — stores and yields oil or gas
Impermeable — prevents upward escape of hydrocarbons

flashcard_questions.q: What are the two properties a reservoir rock must have to store and yield oil?
flashcard_questions.a: High porosity (to store oil) and high permeability (to allow flow).

flashcard_questions.q: What is the role of a cap rock in an oilfield?
flashcard_questions.a: Its low permeability prevents oil and gas from migrating further upward, sealing the trap.

flashcard_questions.q: In what temperature range does oil maturation mainly occur?
Why do oil and gas migrate upward through the crust after being generated?
flashcard_questions.a: They are less dense than the surrounding groundwater, so buoyancy drives upward migration.

flashcard_questions.q: How does an anticline trap oil?
flashcard_questions.a: Oil migrates up into the arch crest; impermeable cap rock draped over the top prevents further escape.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a fault trap in an oilfield?
flashcard_questions.a: A fault that juxtaposes impermeable rock against a reservoir, sealing the migration pathway.

flashcard_questions.q: What is hydraulic fracturing (fracking) designed to extract?
flashcard_questions.a: Oil or gas trapped in tight (very low permeability) source rocks such as shale.

flashcard_questions.q: Why was fracking placed under a moratorium in the UK?
flashcard_questions.a: Induced seismicity caused by high-pressure fluid injection affecting nearby faults.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between porosity and permeability?
flashcard_questions.a: Porosity is total pore space; permeability is the ability of fluids to flow through connected pores.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two rock types commonly found as cap rocks.
What geological event caused the 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill?
flashcard_questions.a: A blowout on an offshore drilling platform in the Gulf of Mexico, releasing ~4.9 million barrels.

glossary_terms.definition: The transformation of buried organic material into oil and gas under increasing heat and pressure in the subsurface.
Fine-grained rock, typically organic-rich mudstone or shale, in which oil and gas are generated by the maturation of buried organic material.
A porous and permeable rock in which oil or gas is stored after migrating from the source rock; typically a sandstone or limestone.
An impermeable rock that prevents oil and gas from migrating further upward, sealing them in the reservoir rock beneath.
A geological structure that prevents upward migration of oil or gas, causing it to accumulate in the reservoir rock beneath the cap rock.
The proportion of a rock's volume made up of pore spaces (gaps between grains); expressed as a percentage.
The ability of a rock to allow fluids to flow through it, controlled by whether the pore spaces are connected.
